title: Chip Security Moves From Checkbox Compliance To Continuous Defense
gist: A DAC roundtable of security leads from Arteris, Cadence, Keysight EDA, Rambus, Siemens EDA, Synaptics, and Synopsys argues hardware security is shifting from checkbox certification to continuous design-deployment-monitoring discipline, with the EU CRA's September 11, 2026 semiconductor deadline (fines up to 4% of annual revenue) as the forcing function, and chiplet verification, hardware SBOMs, and legacy PKA architecture for post-quantum crypto flagged as the hardest open problems.

themes.theme: CRA enforcement as the forcing function

insights.claim: The EU Cyber Resilience Act deadline 'with teeth' for semiconductors is September 11, 2026, per Arteris' Michal Siwinski, making it the near-term compliance event for chipmakers selling into Europe.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Watch for a compliance-spend and security-IP demand bump into the September 2026 CRA deadline, and for any enforcement pause announcements.
insights.quote: For semiconductors, the one that has teeth is September 11 of this year.
insights.locator: SE: What's the CRA deadline?

insights.claim: CRA penalties run around 4% of annual revenue, so liability scales with company size — the bigger the company, the greater the exposure, per Synaptics' Mohit Arora.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Large-cap chip and device vendors face materially larger absolute CRA fine risk than smaller players; security spend is now a liability hedge.
insights.quote: Just to add, the penalties are pretty hefty — like 4% of your annual revenue. So the bigger the company, the greater the liability.
insights.locator: Arora: Just to add, the penalties

insights.claim: The CRA has raised awareness in customer conversations but has not yet demonstrably changed behavior, because no one has been fined yet — enforcement follow-through, not the law itself, will set the security investment level, per Siemens EDA's Chris Giles.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: First CRA fines will be the real catalyst for security spending; until then expect minimal-compliance behavior.
insights.quote: I think it's changed awareness. CRA comes up in a lot of conversations. Has it changed behavior yet? I'm not sure.
insights.locator: Petr: Do you feel like the SSDF

insights.claim: Regulatory deadlines routinely slip once implementation costs become apparent — participants expect the CRA could be paused or changed near its date, as happened with the U.S. SSDF timeline after the government changed.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Do not model CRA compliance revenue as a hard step function; a pause or dilution near the deadline is a live scenario.
insights.quote: you get close to the date, and then the implementation cost becomes apparent, and everybody says, 'Okay, we're going to pause this for a year, we're going to pause this for two years, we're going to change it.'

insights.claim: CRA disclosure obligations cover known vulnerabilities of the whole electronic device — hardware plus software plus anything plugged into it — not just the software stack, which is far broader than most compliance teams assume, and disclosure itself may invite malicious actors to test disclosed weaknesses.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Compliance scope creep favors vendors of hardware-level vulnerability tracking and SBOM tooling; disclosure regimes create a new attack-timing dynamic.
insights.quote: It's not just the software stack of your electronic device, which means software, hardware, whatever else you plug into it. That's the trick.

insights.claim: The CRA has already shifted buying behavior worldwide: customers who used to say 'the customer won't pay for security' can no longer refuse, and companies previously resistant are now putting gigantic roots of trust on chips — bigger than the IP vendors' own solutions — with some bending to OCP designs, per Synopsys' Reed Hinkel.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Root-of-trust silicon area and security IP attach rates are rising structurally; open-source OCP roots of trust may cannibalize some commercial security IP.
insights.quote: companies I thought would never change are putting a gigantic root of trust on a chip — way bigger than any of us have ever built with our own solutions
insights.locator: Hinkel: CRA has been a very

insights.claim: Rambus' Scott Best likens security certification to pre-2008 AAA credit ratings (citing The Big Short): customers buy side-channel protection, PUF technology, and CSIP Level 3 certification as a checkbox to sell into the market, without deploying it well — certification does not prove a product is secure.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A certification-heavy security posture is a red flag, not assurance; expect eventual high-profile breaches at 'certified' vendors to reprice the sector's real security leaders.
insights.quote: 'How could you possibly put a AAA rating on this stuff that you knew was garbage?' And they were like, 'Our customers wouldn't buy it unless it was rated AAA.'
insights.locator: Best: There's an important part about

insights.claim: Chip customers pursue security certification primarily because it is commercially required to sell the product, then filter their A-to-Z security wish list down to a smaller plug-and-play IP to save area and cost, per Cadence's Yathiendra Vunnam.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Security IP demand is certification-driven and cost-constrained; vendors offering right-sized, pre-certified plug-and-play blocks win the design-in.
insights.locator: Vunnam: We've been seeing a lot

insights.claim: Security only gets engineering attention when it is an explicit priority, and priorities only change through incentives — meaning enforcement (sticks) plus revenue upside (carrots), not awareness campaigns.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Track enforcement actions and liability rulings, not standards publications, as the leading indicator of security spending.
insights.quote: You have a stick, and once the stick is applied a few times, everybody else is compelled to avoid the stick.
insights.locator: Siwinski: But it's the usual stuff.

themes.theme: Expanding attack surface: networks, FPGAs, chiplets

insights.claim: As data centers scale from IC to package to board to 'town-sized' fully connected systems, the network — not physical hardware — has become the dominant attack vector, with AI-driven attacks arriving through the network to trigger denials in the system, per Keysight EDA's Alexander Petr.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Network-layer and system-level security (not just chip hardening) is where data-center security spend concentrates; favors test/emulation vendors who can model full systems.
insights.quote: you're basically building town-sized systems that are fully connected everywhere. So the network is becoming one of the bottlenecks where you see a massive number of attacks
insights.locator: Petr: The distinction we need to

insights.claim: The proliferation of FPGAs throughout data-center systems adds programmable logic as an attack surface — software now reaches as deep as the FPGA fabric, so hardware itself becomes exploitable through embedded software rather than physical attack.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: FPGA bitstream and firmware security is an underappreciated exposure in AI infrastructure; a niche for security tooling vendors.
insights.locator: Also, if you look at how the systems are built

insights.claim: Chiplet-based design promises lower device cost via plug-and-play secure subsystems (avoiding advanced nodes for every block, e.g., OCP Caliptra), but the biggest unsolved hurdle is verifying which chiplet is secure and which is not.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Chiplet security attestation/verification is a whitespace market; delays here could slow the multi-vendor chiplet ecosystem investors are counting on.
insights.quote: That's probably the biggest hurdle right now. How do you verify which chiplet is secure and which isn't?

insights.claim: Customers are implementing defense-in-depth with distinct security processing at every OSI networking layer (IPsec, MACsec, etc.), sized for high-performance compute needs.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Per-layer crypto acceleration is becoming a standard silicon cost item in high-compute designs — a tailwind for protocol security IP vendors.
insights.locator: Vunnam: We've been seeing a lot

insights.claim: A software bill of materials for hardware is becoming significantly more important because attacks now enter through embedded software layers driving hardware, and every defense starts with visibility: when a new zero-day drops, most companies cannot even determine whether their systems are impacted.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Hardware-aware SBOM and vulnerability-tracking tooling is a growth category; CRA disclosure duties make it mandatory rather than optional.
insights.quote: Let's say we find a new zero-day vulnerability. Do you know if your system is impacted? How do you know? That alone is already a big challenge.

insights.claim: Malicious actors are actively trying to infiltrate open-source communities to inject back doors, making any open-source component in the hardware/software stack a potential supply-chain threat even when it is believed safe.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Open-source dependency risk now extends to FPGA frameworks and firmware; provenance-scanning vendors benefit.

themes.theme: Security as a price-premium economic engine

insights.claim: Synopsys' Reed Hinkel frames the iPhone as the model of security economics: per-device security investment grew from a few dollars to hundreds of dollars, and the resulting implicit user trust lets it sell for two to three times competitors' prices — security spend is a margin driver when it protects high-value services (PINs, passwords, personal data).
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Security investment correlates with service-revenue business models and pricing power; device makers pivoting to services must raise silicon security spend or face fines/lawsuits.
insights.quote: at the end of the rainbow, they can sell a phone for two or three times what their competitors can because people trust them

insights.claim: Enforcement paths for security failures are bifurcating by geography — government fines in Europe versus lawsuits in the U.S., where courts are already opening the door — and the C-suite is starting to push security requirements down to product managers.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Litigation risk from security failures is an emerging U.S. liability line-item; watch early court rulings as precedent-setters.
insights.quote: In Europe, it's going to be government fines. In the U.S., it's going to be lawsuits. That's just the way it works here.

insights.claim: The U.S. military is a major driver of hardware security investment — the DoD and its suppliers (the Boeings, the Airbuses) constantly push security requirements onto the semiconductor ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Defense-driven security requirements provide a demand floor for hardware security independent of commercial regulation cycles.
insights.locator: Petr: The U.S. military also drives

insights.claim: On post-quantum cryptography, the U.S. executive-order timeline requires PQC algorithms available on products within roughly three years, with full deprecation of legacy crypto about five years out — Synopsys' Hinkel argues the order did not actually pull in dates that were already set.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A three-year product-availability window puts PQC support on current chip design cycles now; security IP vendors with PQC-ready blocks have a near-term catalyst.
insights.quote: you need to have the algorithms available on products. That's a three-year date.
insights.locator: SE: It's still five years out.

insights.claim: The long pole in PQC readiness is not device hardware or firmware but the Public Key Accelerator (PKA) — an ancient 'patch upon patches' technology never designed for deployable, changeable-at-scale crypto — forcing major architecture restructuring to support hybrid post-quantum algorithms.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: PKA rearchitecture is a forced silicon refresh cycle — an opening for new crypto-accelerator IP to displace legacy incumbents.
insights.quote: PKA is ancient technology. It's a patch upon patches. It's a spaghetti work of stuff. It was never organized to be deployable and changeable at scale.
